Neonates of the Ocellated velvet gecko emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs after an incubation period that varies considerably with temperature. For eggs deposited on the thirteenth of June, the incubation duration is approximately fifty-one days when maintained at a constant 28 °C [T = 28 °C], whereas eggs laid on the fourth of April require only thirty-one days [ab = thirty-one days] under identical thermal conditions, a difference likely tied to seasonal variation in the initial developmental state of the fertilised ovum. Upon hatching, these young reptiles possess a snout-vent length of 3.5 cm [Lb = 3.5 cm], and their total length, including the tail, falls between 5.8 and 6 cm. Body mass at emergence is just under one gram, with precise measurements yielding a wet weight of 0.95 grams [Wwb = 0.95 grams], a relatively low value that underscores the species' reliance on yolk reserves during the initial, non-feeding phase of post-hatching life.

As individuals progress through the juvenile and sub-adult stages, their growth trajectories become increasingly shaped by both genetic and environmental factors, culminating in size dimorphism between the sexes. Adult females ultimately achieve a maximum snout-vent length of 9.2 cm [Li = 9.2 cm], which is considerably larger than the ultimate SVL attained by males, measured at 8.5 cm [Li = 8.5 cm]. This divergence in asymptotic body size is typical of many gekkonid lizards and likely reflects differential selective pressures related to fecundity in females and intrasexual competition in males. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight recorded for adults reaches 13 grams [Wwi = 13 grams], a figure that represents the plateau of the species' growth curve and is consistent with the general mass-length relationship observed across similar-sized nocturnal geckos inhabiting rocky outcrops.

Sexual maturation in Oedura monilis is attained when individuals reach a snout-vent length of approximately 6.8 cm [Lp = approximately 6.8 cm], a threshold that marks the onset of gonadal activity and the transition to the reproductively viable adult stage. This size at puberty corresponds to a developmental state where sufficient somatic resources have been accumulated to support the energetic demands of gametogenesis and eventual egg production. Under laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 24 °C [T = 24 °C], females deposit a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] and typically produce two clutches annually [F_R_i = two clutches annually], yielding a maximum annual reproductive output of two eggs per female per year. This modest fecundity is a characteristic feature of the species and aligns with a life-history strategy that prioritises offspring size and parental investment over high numbers of progeny.

Lifespan data for this species, derived from a long-term captive colony held at a stable 24 °C [T = 24 °C], reveal that the oldest documented individuals survive for 17 years [am = 17 years], a remarkable longevity for a gecko of this modest body size. Such an extended maximum lifespan, equivalent to roughly 6205 days, positions Oedura monilis among the longer-lived members of the Diplodactylidae and implies a slow life-history pace characterised by delayed senescence and sustained reproductive capacity well into advanced age. The physiological mechanisms underpinning this longevity, including efficient cellular repair pathways and low basal metabolic rates, remain an active area of investigation, but the demographic data themselves provide a robust framework for understanding the species' overall life-history strategy and its evolutionary trade-offs between current reproduction and future survival.

Beyond the core life-history parameters, several ecologically relevant traits of Oedura monilis merit attention within a comparative physiological context. The species is primarily saxicolous, inhabiting crevices and exfoliating rock sheets in dry sclerophyll forests and woodlands of eastern Australia, where shelters buffer diurnal temperature extremes. Oxygen consumption rates, measured during inactive periods, are consistent with a low-energy lifestyle that helps explain the modest mass gain from a neonatal wet weight of just under 1 gram [Wwb = just under 1 gram] to the 13 gram [Wwi = 13 gram] adult maximum. Field observations also indicate that the 6.8 cm [Lp = 6.8 cm] SVL at puberty is reached within the first two to three years following hatching, a timeframe that aligns well with the species' reproductive schedule and its capacity to exploit predictable seasonal food resources following the summer rains.
